text.English: Why does Aunt Polly have trouble punishing Tom consistently?
Tom tricks or amuses her, and because she loves him as her dead sister’s son, she feels bad both when she spares him and when she hits him.
She believes strict punishment may damage Tom’s spirit, while his occasional obedience makes her question whether discipline is necessary at all.
She struggles because Tom’s offenses change from day to day, and she worries that enforcing Saturday work will make him resent discipline while other boys enjoy their holiday.
She cannot decide whether Tom’s misbehavior comes from deliberate disobedience or childish high spirits, and her fear of ruining him makes punishment feel unfair and painful.

quote.English:
“Hang the boy, can’t I never learn anything? Ain’t he played me tricks
enough like that for me to be looking out for him by this time? But old
fools is the biggest fools there is. Can’t learn an old dog new tricks,
as the saying is. But my goodness, he never plays them alike, two days,
and how is a body to know what’s coming? He ’pears to know just how long
he can torment me before I get my dander up, and he knows if he can make
out to put me off for a minute or make me laugh, it’s all down again and
I can’t hit him a lick. I ain’t doing my duty by that boy, and that’s

text.English: Why did Tom choose to pretend that his sore toe was a serious illness instead of using his loose tooth?

Tom lay thinking. Presently it occurred to him that he wished he was
sick; then he could stay home from school. Here was a vague possibility.
He canvassed his system. No ailment was found, and he investigated
again. This time he thought he could detect colicky symptoms, and he
began to encourage them with considerable hope. But they soon grew
feeble, and presently died wholly away. He reflected further. Suddenly
he discovered something. One of his upper front teeth was loose. This
was lucky; he was about to begin to groan, as a “starter,” as he
called it, when it occurred to him that if he came into court with that
argument, his aunt would pull it out, and that would hurt. So he thought
he would hold the tooth in reserve for the present, and seek further.
Nothing offered for some little time, and then he remembered hearing
the doctor tell about a certain thing that laid up a patient for two or
three weeks and threatened to make him lose a finger. So the boy eagerly
drew his sore toe from under the sheet and held it up for inspection.
But now he did not know the necessary symptoms. However, it seemed
well worth while to chance it, so he fell to groaning with considerable
spirit.

quote.English:
But Tom’s energy did not last. He began to think of the fun he had
planned for this day, and his sorrows multiplied. Soon the free boys
would come tripping along on all sorts of delicious expeditions, and
they would make a world of fun of him for having to work—the very
thought of it burnt him like fire. He got out his worldly wealth and
examined it—bits of toys, marbles, and trash; enough to buy an exchange

of pure freedom. So he returned his straitened means to his pocket, and

text.English: Why was Jackson’s Island a good place for the boys to meet and hide during their escape?

It was uninhabited, wooded, and far from the village near a mostly empty forest.

quote.English:
Three miles below St. Petersburg, at a point where the Mississippi River
was a trifle over a mile wide, there was a long, narrow, wooded island,
with a shallow bar at the head of it, and this offered well as a
rendezvous. It was not inhabited; it lay far over toward the further
shore, abreast a dense and almost wholly unpeopled forest. So Jackson’s
Island was chosen. Who were to be the subjects of their piracies was a
matter that did not occur to them. Then they hunted up Huckleberry Finn,
and he joined them promptly, for all careers were one to him; he was
indifferent. They presently separated to meet at a lonely spot on the
river-bank two miles above the village at the favorite hour—which was
midnight. There was a small log raft there which they meant to capture.
Each would bring hooks and lines, and such provision as he could steal
in the most dark and mysterious way—as became outlaws. And before the
afternoon was done, they had all managed to enjoy the sweet glory of
spreading the fact that pretty soon the town would “hear something.” All
who got this vague hint were cautioned to “be mum and wait.”

text.English: What did Tom and Joe decide was the difference between pretend piracy and real stealing?
They believed stealing sweets and apples was real piracy, while taking meat and other valuable food remained harmless hooking.
They thought taking sweets and apples was just “hooking,” but taking meat and other valuable food was real stealing.

quote.English:
Gradually their talk died out and drowsiness began to steal upon the
eyelids of the little waifs. The pipe dropped from the fingers of the
Red-Handed, and he slept the sleep of the conscience-free and the weary.
The Terror of the Seas and the Black Avenger of the Spanish Main had
more difficulty in getting to sleep. They said their prayers inwardly,
and lying down, since there was nobody there with authority to make them
kneel and recite aloud; in truth, they had a mind not to say them at
all, but they were afraid to proceed to such lengths as that, lest they
might call down a sudden and special thunderbolt from heaven. Then at
once they reached and hovered upon the imminent verge of sleep—but an
intruder came, now, that would not “down.” It was conscience. They began
to feel a vague fear that they had been doing wrong to run away; and
next they thought of the stolen meat, and then the real torture came.
They tried to argue it away by reminding conscience that they had
purloined sweetmeats and apples scores of times; but conscience was not
to be appeased by such thin plausibilities; it seemed to them, in the
end, that there was no getting around the stubborn fact that taking
sweetmeats was only “hooking,” while taking bacon and hams and such
valuables was plain simple stealing—and there was a command against that
in the Bible. So they inwardly resolved that so long as they remained in
the business, their piracies should not again be sullied with the
crime of stealing. Then conscience granted a truce, and these curiously
inconsistent pirates fell peacefully to sleep.

text.English: Why does Huck value living on the island more directly than Tom and Joe do?

The island gives Huck real relief from hunger and bullying, while Tom and Joe mainly enjoy it as a fun escape from school and chores.
The island gives Huck a chance to test himself through dangerous outdoor living, while Tom and Joe mainly appreciate its campfire meals and freedom from daily responsibilities.
The island appeals to Huck because it offers freedom from school and chores, while Tom and Joe value its isolation from town life.

text.English: Why did the villagers give up their plan to punish Injun Joe?
They were afraid of him, and they did not have enough proof to take the case to court.
They believed Muff Potter was responsible, and they worried that punishing Injun Joe would anger the sheriff.
They accepted his version of events, and they feared the villagers would be blamed for false accusations.
They expected the sheriff to handle the matter, and they believed the grave-robbing accusation lacked enough importance for court action.

quote.English:
The villagers had a strong desire to tar-and-feather Injun Joe and ride
him on a rail, for body-snatching, but so formidable was his character
that nobody could be found who was willing to take the lead in the
matter, so it was dropped. He had been careful to begin both of his
inquest-statements with the fight, without confessing the grave-robbery
that preceded it; therefore it was deemed wisest not to try the case in
the courts at present.

text.English: How did omitting the grave robbery from the inquest statements enable the authorities to postpone legal action against Injun Joe?
It made Injun Joe seem merely a witness to the fight, causing authorities to pursue Muff Potter’s case first and defer prosecuting Joe in the courts.
It withheld the evidence connecting Injun Joe to the grave robbery, allowing the authorities to focus on Muff Potter’s alleged involvement and delay taking legal action against Injun Joe.
It made the grave robbery appear unrelated to the murder, leading authorities to investigate the killing separately and postpone questioning Injun Joe.
It allowed Injun Joe’s statements to present the fight as the central event, leaving officials uncertain about his role and persuading them to postpone bringing him before a court.

quote.English:
Close upon the hour of noon the whole village was suddenly electrified
with the ghastly news. No need of the as yet un-dreamed-of telegraph;
the tale flew from man to man, from group to group, from house to house,
with little less than telegraphic speed. Of course the schoolmaster gave
holiday for that afternoon; the town would have thought strangely of
him if he had not.

text.English: Why did Potter say he came back to the graveyard even though he wanted to run away?
He came back because he feared the murdered man’s spirit would follow him if he fled the graveyard.
He said he could not help it and seemed unable to control where he went.
He came back because he wanted to recover his knife before anyone could use it against him.
He returned because he believed witnessing the scene would prove his innocence to the villagers.

quote.English:
“I didn’t do it, friends,” he sobbed; “’pon my word and honor I never
done it.”

text.English: What does Potter’s plea, “Tell ’em, Joe,” show about how Injun Joe controls the story of the murder?
Potter depends on Joe to speak for him, so Joe can control what everyone hears.
Potter assumes Joe will honestly explain events, so Joe gains influence over the villagers’ interpretation.
Potter believes Joe will defend his innocence, allowing Joe to replace the accusation with a different account.
Potter trusts Joe to clarify the confusing evidence, so the villagers can judge Potter fairly.

quote.English:
“Something told me ’t if I didn’t come back and get—” He shuddered; then
waved his nerveless hand with a vanquished gesture and said, “Tell ’em,
Joe, tell ’em—it ain’t any use any more.”

text.English: Why did Injun Joe’s calm story make Tom and Huck afraid to tell what they had seen?
His steady story hid the grave robbery, and his frightening reputation made it feel dangerous to contradict him.
His oath convinced them the villagers already believed him, while their fear of punishment discouraged any confession.
His calm manner suggested innocence, and the boys feared that accusing him would make them appear guilty of the murder.
His oath made them think the court had accepted his version, and their secrecy seemed likely to expose them as accomplices.

quote.English:
Every day or two, during this time of sorrow, Tom watched his
opportunity and went to the little grated jail-window and smuggled such
small comforts through to the “murderer” as he could get hold of. The
jail was a trifling little brick den that stood in a marsh at the edge
of the village, and no guards were afforded for it; indeed, it
was seldom occupied. These offerings greatly helped to ease Tom’s
conscience.

text.English: How did Tom’s guilty secret reveal itself in his sleep and during waking life?
In sleep, he muttered “Don’t torment me so—I’ll tell!”; awake, he avoided the inquests and refused to act as coroner or witness at school.
In his sleep, he tossed about and repeatedly said, “It’s blood, it’s blood, that’s what it is!” When awake, he blanched, dropped his eyes, and shook so badly that he spilled his coffee.

In sleep, he cried out that the murderer should be punished; awake, he steadied himself, met others’ eyes, and confidently presided over the schoolchildren’s inquests without showing unusual distress.

In sleep, he tossed restlessly and repeatedly pleaded that he had seen nothing; awake, he grew pale, avoided conversation, and hurried away whenever the murder was mentioned at breakfast and school that week.

quote.English:
Tom’s fearful secret and gnawing conscience disturbed his sleep for as
much as a week after this; and at breakfast one morning Sid said:

text.English: Why did Tom almost tell the secret at breakfast?
Tom almost told the secret because he mistook Sid’s questions about his nightmares for an invitation to confess the murder.
Tom nearly confessed after Aunt Polly’s concern prompted him to explain why he seemed frightened and distracted.
Tom almost confessed because he believed Sid’s repeated questions about the blood revealed that Sid already knew the truth.
Sid connected Tom’s repeated words about blood and telling with the murder and asked him what he meant.

quote.English: Tom blanched and dropped his eyes.

text.English: When Mary said she had been affected in the same way, how did Sid react, and how did this help Tom?
Sid seemed suspicious, so Tom had to explain his secret openly.
Sid seemed satisfied, so Tom could get away without revealing his secret.
Sid seemed amused, so Tom could dismiss his words as ordinary sleep-talk.
Sid seemed satisfied, so Tom believed his secret had already been discovered.

quote.English:
Mary said she had been affected much the same way. Sid seemed satisfied.
Tom got out of the presence as quick as he plausibly could, and after
that he complained of toothache for a week, and tied up his jaws every
night. He never knew that Sid lay nightly watching, and frequently
slipped the bandage free and then leaned on his elbow listening a good
while at a time, and afterward slipped the bandage back to its place
again. Tom’s distress of mind wore off gradually and the toothache grew
irksome and was discarded. If Sid really managed to make anything out of

text.English: Why did Tom avoid taking part in pretend inquests about dead cats?
They made him fear that others would discover his involvement in the murder.
They reminded him of the testimony he had failed to give, causing shame and anxious discomfort.
They reminded him of the real crime he knew about, making his guilty conscience hurt.
They made him fear that participating in mock inquests might bring supernatural punishment for the murder.

quote.English:
It seemed to Tom that his schoolmates never would get done holding
inquests on dead cats, and thus keeping his trouble present to his mind.
Sid noticed that Tom never was coroner at one of these inquiries,
though it had been his habit to take the lead in all new enterprises;
he noticed, too, that Tom never acted as a witness—and that was strange;
and Sid did not overlook the fact that Tom even showed a marked aversion
to these inquests, and always avoided them when he could. Sid marvelled,

He secretly sent messages to Potter through the jail window.
He smuggled small comforts to Potter through the jail window.
He secretly offered Potter legal advice through the jail window.
He secretly brought food to Potter through a side entrance.

text.English: Why do the younger boys dread school more as Examination Day gets closer?
Because Mr. Dobbins becomes harsher and punishes even small mistakes, making their school days full of fear and suffering.
Because Examination Day requires difficult public performances, and the younger boys fear embarrassing themselves before parents and townspeople.
Because the younger boys must practice longer and endure uncomfortable preparations, making school days exhausting and leaving little time for play.
Because the younger boys are required to sit through older students’ difficult lessons, making school increasingly confusing and discouraging before Examination Day.

quote.English:
Vacation was approaching. The schoolmaster, always severe, grew severer
and more exacting than ever, for he wanted the school to make a good
showing on “Examination” day. His rod and his ferule were seldom idle
now—at least among the smaller pupils. Only the biggest boys, and young
ladies of eighteen and twenty, escaped lashing. Mr. Dobbins’ lashings
were very vigorous ones, too; for although he carried, under his wig, a
perfectly bald and shiny head, he had only reached middle age, and there
was no sign of feebleness in his muscle. As the great day approached,
all the tyranny that was in him came to the surface; he seemed to take a
vindictive pleasure in punishing the least shortcomings. The consequence
was, that the smaller boys spent their days in terror and suffering and
their nights in plotting revenge. They threw away no opportunity to do
the master a mischief. But he kept ahead all the time. The retribution
that followed every vengeful success was so sweeping and majestic that
the boys always retired from the field badly worsted. At last they
conspired together and hit upon a plan that promised a dazzling victory.
They swore in the signpainter’s boy, told him the scheme, and asked his
help. He had his own reasons for being delighted, for the master boarded
in his father’s family and had given the boy ample cause to hate him.
The master’s wife would go on a visit to the country in a few days, and
there would be nothing to interfere with the plan; the master always
prepared himself for great occasions by getting pretty well fuddled, and

text.English: Why does Tom pretend that he is very sick?
So Sid would worry about him.
So he can stay home from school.
So Sid would fetch a doctor and summon Aunt Polly.
So Aunt Polly would pull out his tooth.

quote.English:
Tom lay thinking. Presently it occurred to him that he wished he was
sick; then he could stay home from school. Here was a vague possibility.
He canvassed his system. No ailment was found, and he investigated
again. This time he thought he could detect colicky symptoms, and he
began to encourage them with considerable hope. But they soon grew
feeble, and presently died wholly away. He reflected further. Suddenly
he discovered something. One of his upper front teeth was loose. This
was lucky; he was about to begin to groan, as a “starter,” as he
called it, when it occurred to him that if he came into court with that
argument, his aunt would pull it out, and that would hurt. So he thought
he would hold the tooth in reserve for the present, and seek further.
Nothing offered for some little time, and then he remembered hearing
the doctor tell about a certain thing that laid up a patient for two or
three weeks and threatened to make him lose a finger. So the boy eagerly
drew his sore toe from under the sheet and held it up for inspection.
But now he did not know the necessary symptoms. However, it seemed
well worth while to chance it, so he fell to groaning with considerable
spirit.

text.English: Why did the respectable schoolboys envy Huckleberry Finn’s life?
They believed Huck enjoyed exciting adventures, possessed valuable freedom, attracted admiration, and escaped the ordinary consequences that respectable boys faced at home.
They thought he was free to do what he wanted because he did not have to attend school or church, obey adults, wash, or wear clean clothes.
They envied Huck’s life because he could fish and swim whenever he pleased, sleep wherever he chose, stay up late, fight freely, go barefoot, and swear.
They believed Huck’s poverty protected him from expectations, gave him unusual privacy, encouraged self-reliance, and let him learn about life outside respectable homes and schools.

quote.English:
Shortly Tom came upon the juvenile pariah of the village, Huckleberry
Finn, son of the town drunkard. Huckleberry was cordially hated and
dreaded by all the mothers of the town, because he was idle and lawless
and vulgar and bad—and because all their children admired him so, and
delighted in his forbidden society, and wished they dared to be like
him. Tom was like the rest of the respectable boys, in that he envied
Huckleberry his gaudy outcast condition, and was under strict orders
not to play with him. So he played with him every time he got a chance.
Huckleberry was always dressed in the cast-off clothes of full-grown
men, and they were in perennial bloom and fluttering with rags. His hat
was a vast ruin with a wide crescent lopped out of its brim; his coat,
when he wore one, hung nearly to his heels and had the rearward buttons
far down the back; but one suspender supported his trousers; the seat of
the trousers bagged low and contained nothing, the fringed legs dragged
in the dirt when not rolled up.

text.English: What prank did the students and the signpainter’s boy carry out against the schoolmaster during Examination Evening?
While the drunken schoolmaster napped, they painted his bald head gold, replaced his wig, and then lowered a cat that seized the wig and pulled it off in front of the audience.
While the drunken schoolmaster napped, they painted his bald head gold, replaced his wig, then lowered a dog that dragged it away before the audience.

While the drunken schoolmaster napped, they painted his bald head gold, replaced his wig, and lowered a cat that startled him awake, making him drop the wig before the audience.

text.English: How did Tom’s public punishment reinforce school discipline while also becoming a source of pleasure and status for him?

Being sent to sit with the girls publicly embarrassed him and warned him against misbehavior, but it also placed him beside Becky, whose interest in his drawing and request for lessons gave him exciting attention and social status.

Being sent to sit with the girls publicly embarrassed him and reminded him that misbehavior brought humiliating consequences, but it also let him enjoy the excitement of occupying the girls’ side, where Becky’s curiosity about his drawing made him feel mature and admired despite the teacher’s intended warning.
Being sent to sit with the girls publicly embarrassed Tom and demonstrated the master’s authority, but it also elevated him socially because the other pupils envied his special position beside Becky.

Being sent to sit with the girls publicly embarrassed him and showed that the master controlled his behavior, but it also let him impress Becky with his drawing, secure her promise to stay at noon, and feel important among the pupils.

quote.English: “Now, sir, go and sit with the girls! And let this be a warning to you.”

text.English: How did the audience’s applause affect the little boy and the girl after their performances?
The little boy was still cruelly frightened despite receiving strong applause, while the girl finished her performance flushed and happy after receiving applause.
The little boy overcame his fear when the audience applauded, while the girl became nervous and embarrassed after receiving enthusiastic applause.
The little boy grew more frightened after applause, while the girl accepted the applause calmly but showed no particular happiness.

text.English: How does the teacher’s rigid persistence in redrawing the map satirize the school’s demand for orderly public performances?
His repeated redrawing suggests that public ceremonies can be rescued through stricter technical control, turning the teacher’s concern for map accuracy into a comic substitute for genuine success.
His careful mapmaking celebrates the teacher’s confidence that orderly correction can preserve the ceremony’s dignity, despite awkward execution and the audience’s distracting laughter throughout.
His repeated corrections mock the belief that disciplined repetition can restore an impressive performance, even when visible mistakes make the audience increasingly amused.
His mechanical persistence parodies the pressure to keep a public exercise going as if it were succeeding, even while the performance visibly fails and the audience laughs.

Now the master, mellow almost to the verge of geniality, put his chair
aside, turned his back to the audience, and began to draw a map of
America on the blackboard, to exercise the geography class upon. But he
made a sad business of it with his unsteady hand, and a smothered titter
rippled over the house. He knew what the matter was, and set himself to
right it. He sponged out lines and remade them; but he only distorted
them more than ever, and the tittering was more pronounced. He threw his
entire attention upon his work, now, as if determined not to be put down
by the mirth. He felt that all eyes were fastened upon him; he imagined
he was succeeding, and yet the tittering continued; it even manifestly
increased. And well it might. There was a garret above, pierced with
a scuttle over his head; and down through this scuttle came a cat,
suspended around the haunches by a string; she had a rag tied about
her head and jaws to keep her from mewing; as she slowly descended she
curved upward and clawed at the string, she swung downward and clawed
at the intangible air. The tittering rose higher and higher—the cat was
within six inches of the absorbed teacher’s head—down, down, a little
lower, and she grabbed his wig with her desperate claws, clung to it,
and was snatched up into the garret in an instant with her trophy still
in her possession! And how the light did blaze abroad from the master’s
bald pate—for the signpainter’s boy had _gilded_ it!

text.English: Why did the students’ “original” compositions seem formulaic instead of truly individual?
They lacked enough education to organize original ideas, so they relied on simple stock expressions.
They repeated familiar themes and used the same inherited style, fancy language, and moral sermons.
They followed fashionable subjects, copied admired authors, favored dramatic imagery, and imitated public-speaking conventions.
They copied their mothers’ opinions, borrowed familiar plots, arranged predictable conclusions, and avoided personal experiences.

quote.English:
“The Boy Stood on the Burning Deck” followed; also “The Assyrian Came
Down,” and other declamatory gems. Then there were reading exercises,
and a spelling fight. The meagre Latin class recited with honor. The
prime feature of the evening was in order, now—original “compositions”
by the young ladies. Each in her turn stepped forward to the edge of the
platform, cleared her throat, held up her manuscript (tied with dainty
ribbon), and proceeded to read, with labored attention to “expression”
and punctuation. The themes were the same that had been illuminated upon
similar occasions by their mothers before them, their grandmothers, and
doubtless all their ancestors in the female line clear back to the
Crusades. “Friendship” was one; “Memories of Other Days”; “Religion in
History”; “Dream Land”; “The Advantages of Culture”; “Forms of Political
Government Compared and Contrasted”; “Melancholy”; “Filial Love”; “Heart
Longings,” etc., etc.

text.English: How did the schoolgirls’ compositions make ordinary subjects seem falsely serious?
They used exaggerated sadness, worn-out fancy words, and a forced moral sermon at the end.
They treated routine experiences as historical crises, supported claims with learned references, and concluded with sincere personal reflections.
They described minor happenings in solemn, elevated language and connected them to broad philosophical themes.
They used fearful warnings, technical vocabulary, and an uplifting personal reflection to elevate ordinary subjects.

quote.English:
A prevalent feature in these compositions was a nursed and petted
melancholy; another was a wasteful and opulent gush of “fine language”;
another was a tendency to lug in by the ears particularly prized words
and phrases until they were worn entirely out; and a peculiarity that
conspicuously marked and marred them was the inveterate and intolerable
sermon that wagged its crippled tail at the end of each and every one of
them. No matter what the subject might be, a brainracking effort was
made to squirm it into some aspect or other that the moral and religious
mind could contemplate with edification. The glaring insincerity of
these sermons was not sufficient to compass the banishment of the
fashion from the schools, and it is not sufficient today; it never will
be sufficient while the world stands, perhaps. There is no school in all
our land where the young ladies do not feel obliged to close their
compositions with a sermon; and you will find that the sermon of the
most frivolous and the least religious girl in the school is always the
longest and the most relentlessly pious. But enough of this. Homely
truth is unpalatable.

text.English: When listeners praised writing filled with fancy phrases like “beauteous” and “life’s page,” what were they rewarding?
They rewarded emotional sincerity and moral insight over polished language.
They rewarded impressive delivery and solemn performance over thoughtful, original writing.
They rewarded polished vocabulary and conventional themes as signs of literary excellence.
A showy, familiar style more than original and meaningful ideas.

quote.English:
This nightmare occupied some ten pages of manuscript and wound up with a
sermon so destructive of all hope to non-Presbyterians that it took
the first prize. This composition was considered to be the very finest
effort of the evening. The mayor of the village, in delivering the prize
to the author of it, made a warm speech in which he said that it was by
far the most “eloquent” thing he had ever listened to, and that Daniel
Webster himself might well be proud of it.

text.English: Why did Tom and Huck decide to wait before exploring the haunted house?
They feared the haunted house was occupied, so they chose to return when they had more daylight.
They believed Friday and Huck’s bad dream about rats were signs of trouble, so they postponed it.
They believed Saturday was unlucky and thought rats brought treasure hunters bad luck, so they postponed exploring until Sunday.
They believed the house was safest at noon, so they postponed exploring until Saturday afternoon.

quote.English:
“Well, I didn’t neither, but all at once it popped onto me that it was
Friday.”

They wanted to prove the haunted house was truly full of riches.
Finding some gold could make them believe that more treasure was nearby.
They believed the coins had been planted as a test, with greater rewards awaiting persistent hunters.
They assumed the coins proved that a famous gang had hidden treasure nearby.

quote.English: “No—but I’d say come in the night as we used to do—it’s better.”

text.English: Why did the haunted house feel threatening to the boys?
Its rumors of ghosts, dark interior, hidden passages, and fear of being trapped inside made the house seem dangerous and frightening.

Its distance from town, unfamiliar surroundings, possible criminals, and uncertainty about finding treasure made the house seem dangerous and frightening.
Its dead silence, lonely setting, decaying rooms, and signs that people had abandoned it made the house seem dangerous and frightening.

quote.English:
When they reached the haunted house there was something so weird and
grisly about the dead silence that reigned there under the baking sun,
and something so depressing about the loneliness and desolation of the
place, that they were afraid, for a moment, to venture in. Then they
crept to the door and took a trembling peep. They saw a weedgrown,
floorless room, unplastered, an ancient fireplace, vacant windows,
a ruinous staircase; and here, there, and everywhere hung ragged and
abandoned cobwebs. They presently entered, softly, with quickened
pulses, talking in whispers, ears alert to catch the slightest sound,
and muscles tense and ready for instant retreat.

text.English: How did spending more time in the haunted house change the boys’ feelings about it?
They remained frightened, searched cautiously, and doubted whether their courage was genuine.
They became less afraid, examined it more confidently, and even admired their own bravery.
They grew more curious, explored further, and forgot that the house had seemed frightening at first.
They became accustomed to the ruins, dismissed the house as harmless, and stopped respecting its frightening atmosphere.

It convinced them that abandoned houses commonly contained forgotten fortunes, so searching old buildings seemed more promising than before.
It convinced them that treasure hunting would bring fame and adventure, while the hidden coins proved their luck was changing.

chance at that job; accidents might happen; ’tain’t in such a very good
place; we’ll just regularly bury it—and bury it deep.”

text.English: How did exploring many winding passages make it hard for Tom and Becky to return?
The bats drove them into unfamiliar corridors, and Tom followed the wrong branches while trying to avoid returning past them.

The passages became narrower and darker, and their candles burned out before Tom could remember the route.

guidance, and started upon their quest. They wound this way and that,
far down into the secret depths of the cave, made another mark, and
branched off in search of novelties to tell the upper world about. In
one place they found a spacious cavern, from whose ceiling depended a
multitude of shining stalactites of the length and circumference of
a man’s leg; they walked all about it, wondering and admiring, and
presently left it by one of the numerous passages that opened into
it. This shortly brought them to a bewitching spring, whose basin was
incrusted with a frostwork of glittering crystals; it was in the midst
of a cavern whose walls were supported by many fantastic pillars which
had been formed by the joining of great stalactites and stalagmites
together, the result of the ceaseless water-drip of centuries. Under the
roof vast knots of bats had packed themselves together, thousands in a
bunch; the lights disturbed the creatures and they came flocking down by
hundreds, squeaking and darting furiously at the candles. Tom knew their
ways and the danger of this sort of conduct. He seized Becky’s hand and
hurried her into the first corridor that offered; and none too soon, for
a bat struck Becky’s light out with its wing while she was passing out
of the cavern. The bats chased the children a good distance; but the
fugitives plunged into every new passage that offered, and at last got
rid of the perilous things. Tom found a subterranean lake, shortly,
which stretched its dim length away until its shape was lost in the
shadows. He wanted to explore its borders, but concluded that it would
be best to sit down and rest awhile, first. Now, for the first time, the
deep stillness of the place laid a clammy hand upon the spirits of the

branched off in search of novelties to tell the upper world about. In

multitude of shining stalactites of the length and circumference of
a man’s leg; they walked all about it, wondering and admiring, and
presently left it by one of the numerous passages that opened into
it. This shortly brought them to a bewitching spring, whose basin was
incrusted with a frostwork of glittering crystals; it was in the midst
of a cavern whose walls were supported by many fantastic pillars which
had been formed by the joining of great stalactites and stalagmites
together, the result of the ceaseless water-drip of centuries. Under the
roof vast knots of bats had packed themselves together, thousands in a
bunch; the lights disturbed the creatures and they came flocking down by
hundreds, squeaking and darting furiously at the candles. Tom knew their
ways and the danger of this sort of conduct. He seized Becky’s hand and
hurried her into the first corridor that offered; and none too soon, for
a bat struck Becky’s light out with its wing while she was passing out
of the cavern. The bats chased the children a good distance; but the
fugitives plunged into every new passage that offered, and at last got
rid of the perilous things. Tom found a subterranean lake, shortly,
which stretched its dim length away until its shape was lost in the
shadows. He wanted to explore its borders, but concluded that it would

quote.English:
Tuesday afternoon came, and waned to the twilight. The village of St.
Petersburg still mourned. The lost children had not been found. Public
prayers had been offered up for them, and many and many a private prayer
that had the petitioner’s whole heart in it; but still no good news came
from the cave. The majority of the searchers had given up the quest
and gone back to their daily avocations, saying that it was plain the
children could never be found. Mrs. Thatcher was very ill, and a great
part of the time delirious. People said it was heartbreaking to hear her
call her child, and raise her head and listen a whole minute at a time,
then lay it wearily down again with a moan. Aunt Polly had drooped into
a settled melancholy, and her gray hair had grown almost white. The
village went to its rest on Tuesday night, sad and forlorn.
